question: Which type of circuit is used to convert both the half-cycles of an AC waveform into a pulsating DC waveform?
solution:
__**Explanation:**__

A full-wave rectifier works by using either a center-tapped transformer along with two diodes (in the case of a center-tapped configuration) or a bridge rectifier consisting of four diodes. The primary objective is to ensure that the output voltage during both the positive and negative half-cycles of the AC input is unidirectional.

 
• During the **positive half-cycle** of the AC input, the diode(s) in the circuit allow current to flow through the load in one direction, resulting in a positive output voltage.
 
• During the **negative half-cycle** of the AC input, a different set of diode(s) conducts, effectively inverting the polarity of the negative half-cycle to produce a positive output voltage.

As a result, the output waveform consists of a series of positive pulses corresponding to both half-cycles of the AC input, making the full-wave rectifier far more efficient than a half-wave rectifier.

**Advantages:**

 
• Utilizes both half-cycles of the AC input, doubling the efficiency compared to half-wave rectifiers.
 
• Produces a higher average output voltage and current.
 
• Reduces ripple frequency in the output waveform, making it easier to smooth the DC output using a filter.
 
• More suitable for applications requiring higher power output.

**Applications:**

 
• Used in power supplies to convert AC mains into DC voltage for electronic devices.
 
• Commonly employed in battery charging circuits.
 
• Used in DC motor drives and other industrial applications requiring DC voltage.

**Correct Option Analysis:**

The correct option is:

**Option 4:** Full-wave rectifier

A full-wave rectifier is explicitly designed to convert both the positive and negative half-cycles of an AC waveform into a pulsating DC waveform. This makes it the most efficient type of rectifier for this purpose. By utilizing both half-cycles, the full-wave rectifier ensures a continuous and smoother output, making it ideal for applications requiring stable DC voltage
